alignment.note: The Syriac ܘܣܠܩ fuses the conjunction and verb ('and-he-went-up') into a single graphic unit, hence it is grouped with both καί and ἀνέβη; the action 'went up' is common to all three.
Greek πρὸς αὐτοὺς and Latin ad illos render the prepositional phrase 'to them' analytically, while Syriac ܠܘܬܗܘܢ expresses the same with a single inflected preposition-plus-suffix form.

Greek εἰς τὸ πλοῖον and Latin in navim render 'into the boat' with preposition plus noun; Syriac ܠܣܦܝܢܬܐ uses the dative-locative ܠ- prefix on the noun alone, a normal Syriac construction lacking a separate article.

The Syriac ܘܫܠܝܬ ('and it ceased/grew still') again conflates conjunction and verb; the verb κοπάζω ('abated') and cessavit are matched here, with the conjunction already counted in the preceding stretch as part of the fused form.
Greek ὁ ἄνεμος and Latin ventus carry an explicit article/marked noun; Syriac ܪܘܚܐ ('the wind') uses the emphatic state to convey definiteness without a separate article.

Greek piles up an emphatic intensifier λίαν ἐκ περισσοῦ ('exceedingly beyond measure'); Latin renders this with plus magis, while Syriac compresses it to the single adverb ܛܒ ('greatly'), losing the redundant doubling characteristic of Markan emphasis.

Greek ἐξίσταντο (imperfect) and Latin stupebant render the durative 'were amazed'; Syriac uses a periphrastic participle plus auxiliary ܡܬܕܡܪܝܢ ܗܘܘ to express the same continuous past aspect, an idiomatic Syriac equivalent of the Greek imperfect.

Greek attests a second coordinate verb καὶ ἐθαύμαζον ('and marvelled'), doubling the verbs of astonishment; the Vulgate omits this entirely, while Syriac renders only a single coordinated participle ܘܬܗܝܪܝܢ ('and astonished'), so neither version preserves the full Greek verbal pair.

Greek ἐν ἑαυτοῖς and Latin intra se render the reflexive phrase 'within themselves'; Syriac ܒܢܦܫܗܘܢ ('in their soul/self') employs the noun nap̄šā with possessive suffix as its standard reflexive idiom.
